The problem

Generic course sites don’t speak “clinician”.

Medical staff need accredited learning for their own field, a clear count of CME points, and proof they finished. That was scattered across platforms built for everyone.

My bet

Ask who they are first, then answer “does this count for me?” everywhere.

A 3-step setup by designation and specialty, then CME points, time and rating on every course card.

What I designed

One system, four apps.

The learner mobile app, the learner web app, a business (team) web app, and an admin studio for building and publishing courses.

How I work with AI

ChatGPT and Claude in research.

To draft interview guides and surveys, cluster what I heard into themes, and summarise the competitor teardown. See how ↓

    01 · What clinicians told us

    Doctors don’t browse for fun. They look for credits that count.

    The client wanted one place for medical professionals to learn and earn continuing education (CME) points. Before any screens, I needed to understand how clinicians actually pick a course, and why they drop one.

    I ran stakeholder workshops with the client team, interviews with clinicians, and a short survey, then did a competitor teardown of the platforms they already used. ChatGPT and Claude helped me plan and synthesise. The conversations were mine.

    Short version: every screen has to answer “is this for me, and does it count?”

    🩺

    Relevance beats volume

    A nurse and a surgeon need very different catalogues. Generic “popular” lists made people scroll past most of what they saw.

    🏅

    Credits are the currency

    People judged a course by its CME points, length and who teaches it, so that information had to be visible before opening anything.

    📜

    Proof has to be easy

    Finishing isn’t the end. A certificate has to be easy to find, download and share, with a clear validity period.

    Competitor teardownFrom the research board · what I kept and what I avoided
    02 · One product, four doors

    I mapped the whole system before polishing any one screen.

    Learners would use the app on shift breaks and the web at a desk. Hospitals would buy seats through a business plan. Educators and the client team needed somewhere to build courses. That’s four apps sharing one set of courses, points and certificates.

    So the information architecture came first: Explore, My Learning, Purchases and Certificates work the same way everywhere, and the admin studio follows the order a course is built in: categories → details → modules → assessment → preview → publish.

    03 · Decision log

    Six calls that shaped the product

    Each card is a real fork in the road: what I chose, what I rejected, and why. Open one to see the screens behind it.

    01Show the catalogue first, or ask who they are?Ask first, allow skip

    Rejected: dropping new users into a generic catalogue and hoping search does the rest.

    Chose: a 3-step setup with a progress bar: designation (physician, nurse, dentist and more), then specialty, then a short profile. Every step can be skipped.

    Why: relevance was the top theme in research. Two taps buy a home screen that already speaks their language, and Skip keeps it from becoming a gate.

    02What does a course card need to say?“Does it count?”

    Rejected: image-and-title cards like a general course site.

    Chose: CME points lead the card, followed by rating and review count, title, educator, a short summary, total time and student count.

    Why: clinicians judge a course by its credits and time cost. Putting that on the card saves opening five courses to compare them.

    03One price, or several ways to pay?Course, category or unlimited

    Rejected: per-course purchase only, which gets expensive for people who need many credits a year.

    Chose: buy one course, subscribe to a category (the course page shows the saving), or go unlimited. Each has its own receipt type in My Purchases.

    Why: a nurse topping up a few points and a specialist doing a full year of CPD have different budgets. The upsell lives right under the price, not in a pop-up.

    04Custom video player, or the native one?Native for lessons

    First version: a custom in-page preview player with our own controls.

    Chose: the system player for lessons, with picture-in-picture, AirPlay and ±10s skip. The custom player stays only for the short course preview before purchase.

    Why: people watch on breaks and on the move. Native controls are familiar, accessible and cheaper to build well than our own.

    05What happens after a wrong answer?Teach, don’t just mark

    Rejected: a score and nothing else.

    Chose: a results page that shows the grade and CME points, then every question with correct or incorrect. Wrong answers link straight to “Learn again by watching course”, with Try again at the bottom.

    Why: the goal is competence, not just a pass mark. Sending people back to the exact lesson turns a fail into a next step.

    06Is a certificate the end of the journey?Make it shareable

    Rejected: a PDF buried in a profile menu.

    Chose: a certificate view with the owner, a validity period, the course it belongs to, Share to LinkedIn and Download. Courses can also be gifted with a personal note.

    Why: proof of learning matters for careers and compliance. Sharing and gifting also bring new learners in without paid ads.

    05 · How I use AI now

    AI speeds up the research. The judgement stays human.

    On this project I used ChatGPT and Claude as research assistants: to prepare, to make sense of a lot of notes quickly, and to compare competitors. I ran every conversation, checked every theme against the raw notes, and made every design call.

    ✦PrepareChatGPT · Claude

    Drafted interview guides and survey questions, which I edited for tone and medical context.

    ✓ListenMe

    Stakeholder workshops, clinician interviews and the survey.

    ⌘Make senseClaude · ChatGPT

    Clustered notes and open answers into themes, and summarised the competitor teardown into a matrix.

    ◎Check & decideMe

    Verified each theme against raw notes, dropped the weak ones, and turned the rest into design principles.

    ✎DesignMe · Figma

    IA, wireframes, UI and prototype across all four apps.

    What the AI did

    • First drafts of interview guides and survey questions
    • Grouped notes and open answers into candidate themes
    • Turned my teardown notes into a comparison matrix

    What I did

    • Ran the workshops, interviews and survey
    • Checked every theme against the raw notes, and cut the weak ones
    • Used each competitor myself to verify the matrix
    • Designed the IA, flows, UI and prototype for all four apps

    “AI is quick at finding patterns. It’s my job to know which ones are real.”

    06 · Results, honestly

    How I’d know it’s working

    I don’t have post-launch numbers I can share, so I won’t make any up. These are the metrics I set out to track, and the question each one answers.

    Setup completionNew users who finish designation and specialty, compared with those who skipIs personalising worth two taps?
    Time to first lessonFrom sign-up to pressing play on a first lessonDoes relevance speed people up?
    Retry → passPeople who fail, use “Learn again”, then pass on the next tryDoes the feedback teach?
    Certificate sharesShares and downloads per completed courseDoes proof bring people back?

    Clinicians don’t need more content. They need the right content, and proof they did it.

    What I learned

    Designing four apps at once only works if the core objects (courses, points, certificates) behave the same everywhere. Getting the IA right early saved more time than any single screen.

    Risks I watched

    • Onboarding fatigue: kept to 3 steps, all skippable
    • Pricing confusion across three ways to buy
    • AI themes sounding confident on thin evidence

    What I’d do next

    • Usability test onboarding and checkout with clinicians
    • Design reminders for expiring certificates
    • Add search filters by CME points and duration
